items.topic: Antidepressants/SSRIs — monitor and report increased suicidal ideation especially early in treatment and in younger clients
items.stem: A 19-year-old client starts a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for major depression. Which teaching point is the highest priority in the first weeks of therapy?

options.text: Immediately notify the provider of worsening depression or new or increased suicidal thoughts
Stop the SSRI after 3 days if mood has not fully returned to normal
Combine the SSRI with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) to speed recovery
Skip doses on weekends to reduce the risk of sexual side effects

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: clients must immediately notify the provider about increased depression or suicidal ideation; FDA boxed warning notes increased suicidal thoughts/behaviour risk in children, adolescents, and young adults under 24. Merck: suicide risk may rise early in antidepressant treatment; carefully monitor for suicidal behaviours and ideation.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Therapeutic effects often take about 2 weeks to begin and 4–6 weeks for full effect; abrupt early stopping is not appropriate teaching.
rationales.C: Incorrect. SSRIs must not be combined with MAOIs because of serotonin syndrome risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Skipping doses is unsafe and unrelated to priority suicide-risk monitoring.

items.topic: NGN matrix — antidepressant/SSRI safety teaching indicated vs not
items.stem: For a young adult starting an SSRI, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Report new or worsening suicidal thoughts to the provider right away
Expect full antidepressant benefit within 24 hours of the first dose
Continue prescribed therapy while mood and anxiety are monitored over weeks
Start an MAOI the same day as the SSRI to boost effect
Know that suicidal ideation risk is a particular concern in adolescents and young adults

rationales.R1: Indicated. Immediate reporting of suicidal ideation is required teaching.
rationales.R2: Not indicated. Onset is typically weeks, not one day.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Ongoing monitoring of mood/anxiety during treatment is recommended.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Concurrent MAOI + SSRI risks serotonin syndrome.
rationales.R5: Indicated. Boxed warning / evidence focus includes children, adolescents, and young adults.

items.topic: NGN cloze — SSRI onset timing and suicide-ideation reporting
items.stem: Complete the teaching for a client newly prescribed an SSRI.

ngn.template: Full therapeutic effects of an SSRI often take about {B1}. The client should {B2} if depression worsens or suicidal thoughts appear.

B1.text: immediately after combining with an MAOI

B2.text: double the next dose without calling
stop all fluids until mood improves
wait at least 3 months before telling anyone

rationales.B1a: Correct. OpenStax: about 2 weeks to begin seeing effects and 4–6 weeks for full therapeutic effects.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Antidepressant benefit is not expected within hours of the first dose.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Missed doses are not the measure of therapeutic onset.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Combining with an MAOI is contraindicated.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Clients must immediately notify the provider about increased depression or suicidal ideations.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Dose changes require provider direction.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Fluid restriction is unrelated and unsafe teaching.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Delaying reporting of suicidal thoughts is dangerous.

items.topic: Autism spectrum disorder — support predictable routines and reduce overwhelming sensory input
items.stem: A school-age client with autism spectrum disorder becomes distressed when the unit lighting, noise, and schedule change abruptly. Which nursing action best supports the client?

options.text: Reduce unnecessary noise and bright stimuli when possible, keep routines predictable, and allow preferred communication supports
Force prolonged eye contact and hugs so the client learns typical social behaviour
Suddenly rearrange meals, clothing, and procedures to increase flexibility
Ignore sensory distress because it is attention-seeking and should be extinguished

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: families/nurses adapt with sensory considerations, routines, and communication supports (including pictures/devices). Merck: extreme over- or under-reaction to sensory input and inflexible adherence to routines are core features; supportive environments reduce distress.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Forced eye contact or unwanted touch can be aversive for sensory-sensitive clients.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Abrupt routine changes often increase extreme distress.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sensory distress is a recognized ASD feature, not mere attention-seeking.

items.topic: Postpartum perineal comfort — ice packs in the first 24 hours to reduce swelling and pain
items.stem: A client is 6 hours after a vaginal birth with perineal swelling and discomfort. Which comfort measure is most appropriate now?

options.text: Apply an ice or cold pack to the perineum during the first 24 hours to reduce swelling and pain
Begin prolonged hot tub soaks immediately after delivery before any cold therapy
Avoid all perineal cleansing until the 6-week postpartum visit
Encourage the client to sit continuously on a hard chair to promote drainage

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: ice/cold packs for the first 24 hours (table also notes early postpartum cold application). MedlinePlus: ice packs in the first 24 hours decrease swelling and help pain. Merck: immediately after delivery, ice packs may help reduce pain and edema; warm sitz baths are used later.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Warm baths/sitz are typically deferred until after the early cold period (about 24 hours).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Perineal hygiene (e.g., peri-bottle rinsing) is taught during the postpartum stay.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Hard prolonged sitting increases discomfort; cushioning/limited sitting is preferred.

sources.evidence: Ice/cold packs to perineum for first 24 hours; warm sitz baths; peri-bottle; avoid long hard sitting.

items.topic: Circumcision aftercare — petroleum jelly to prevent diaper sticking; monitor bleeding and voiding
items.stem: Parents ask how to care for their newborn after circumcision. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Apply petroleum jelly to the penis or diaper area with diaper changes so the healing site does not stick
Scrub the incision vigorously with antiseptic soap at every diaper change
Leave the site dry with no ointment so a hard scab forms faster
Ignore small amounts of yellow crust because infection is inevitable after circumcision

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: gauze with petroleum jelly on the tip/diaper prevents sticking; continue dab of petroleum jelly during healing. MedlinePlus: apply petroleum jelly after diaper changes to protect the healing incision; yellow crust can be normal.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Vigorous scrubbing can disrupt healing; gentle cleansing is taught.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Petroleum jelly is used specifically to protect the site and prevent diaper adherence.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Mild yellow crust may be normal healing, but infection is not inevitable and concerning signs need evaluation.

sources.title: 24.1 Basic Newborn Care
sources.evidence: Petroleum jelly gauze on tip/diaper; yellow discharge/crust may be normal healing; report active bleeding.

sources.publisher: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
sources.evidence: Apply petroleum jelly after diaper changes; some swelling and yellow crust normal.

items.jurisdiction_note: CPS/CFPC recommend routine IM vitamin K for all newborns in Canada; oral regimens only if parents decline IM and are counselled that oral is less protective.
items.topic: Newborn vitamin K IM prophylaxis to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding
items.stem: Parents ask why their healthy term newborn is offered a vitamin K injection soon after birth. Which explanation is best?

options.text: A single intramuscular vitamin K dose helps prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which can cause serious hemorrhage
Vitamin K is given only to treat already-diagnosed jaundice and has no preventive role
Oral vitamin K once at birth is proven more effective than intramuscular vitamin K for late bleeding prevention
Vitamin K injections are unnecessary for breastfed newborns because breast milk is high in vitamin K

rationales.A: Correct. CPS: routine IM vitamin K effectively prevents VKDB; recommended for all newborns. Merck: phytonadione IM within 6 hours prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Vitamin K prophylaxis is preventive, not a jaundice treatment.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CPS states oral regimens are less effective than IM, especially for late VKDB.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Breast milk is relatively low in vitamin K; exclusively breastfed infants are at risk for late VKDB without prophylaxis.

items.topic: Caput succedaneum crosses suture lines; cephalohematoma is limited by sutures (subperiosteal)
items.stem: A newborn has scalp swelling after a long vaginal birth. Which finding best supports caput succedaneum rather than cephalohematoma?

options.text: Soft boggy edema that crosses cranial suture lines
A firm swelling sharply limited to one cranial bone that does not cross sutures
A fluctuant mass extending into the neck with signs of shock
Absence of any scalp changes because molding never involves fluid

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: caput is soft/boggy edema that crosses suture lines. Merck: caput typically crosses suture lines.
rationales.B: Incorrect. That pattern describes cephalohematoma (subperiosteal, limited by sutures).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Extension with possible shock suggests subgaleal hemorrhage, a different emergency.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Caput and molding-related extracranial collections are common after birth.

sources.title: 23.1 Physical Assessment of the Newborn
sources.section: Abnormal Variations Commonly Occurring in Newborns
sources.evidence: Caput crosses sutures, soft/boggy; cephalohematoma deeper, does not cross suture lines.

sources.title: Birth Injuries
sources.evidence: Caput crosses suture lines; cephalhematoma limited by periosteum at sutures; subgaleal can cause significant blood loss.

items.topic: NGN cloze — powdered formula: measure water first; never microwave
items.stem: Complete safe powdered infant formula teaching for parents.

ngn.template: When mixing powdered formula, always {B1}. If warming is desired, {B2}.

B1.text: measure the water first, then add the powder per label
add extra water beyond the label to prevent constipation
guess scoop amounts without reading the can
mix leftover bottle formula back into the can for later

B2.text: warm under running water or in a warm water bath — never microwave
microwave on high for 2 minutes to sterilize
boil the prepared bottle for 30 minutes after every feed
add boiling oil to raise temperature quickly

rationales.B1a: Correct. CDC and OpenStax: always measure water first, then add powder per instructions.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Extra water dilutes nutrients; too little water can strain kidneys.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Exact labeled amounts are required.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Leftover formula after feeding is discarded, not returned to the can.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Never microwave; uneven hot spots can burn the infant. Warm under/in warm water and wrist-test.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Microwaving creates dangerous hot spots.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Overheating prepared bottles this way is not standard teaching and risks burns/nutrient damage.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Unsafe and unrelated to formula warming.

sources.title: 24.1 Basic Newborn Care
sources.section: Safe Preparation of Formula in the Hospital / Competency: Safety: Preparing Powdered Infant Formula
sources.evidence: Measure water first then add powder; never warm in microwave; discard leftovers after feeding.

sources.evidence: Always measure water first then add powder; never use a microwave because of hot spots.

items.jurisdiction_note: CPS Caring for Kids water safety aligns with CDC drowning prevention on constant supervision; Canada-focused parent teaching.
items.topic: Drowning prevention — constant adult supervision; never leave child alone in bathtub or near water
items.stem: A parent of a toddler asks how to prevent drowning at home. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Never leave a child alone in a bathtub or near water, even briefly; keep toddlers within arm’s reach of an adult
Bath seats make constant adult supervision unnecessary during tub time
Children can be left alone if older siblings are watching from another room
Water wings alone are approved safety devices that replace lifejackets and adult supervision

rationales.A: Correct. CPS: toddlers within arm’s reach; never leave alone in pool/bathtub even for a moment. CDC: designate close constant supervision including bathtubs; drowning is often silent and fast.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Bath seats give false security; supervision remains mandatory (CPS household safety teaching).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Other children do not replace adult supervision.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Water wings/foam toys are not safety devices; supervision and proper flotation as indicated still apply.

sources.publisher: Canadian Paediatric Society — Caring for Kids
sources.evidence: Toddlers within arm’s reach; never leave alone in bathtub/pool; water wings are not safety devices.

sources.evidence: Constant close supervision in/near water including bathtubs; do not rely on air-filled or foam toys as safety devices.
